title: Adrenal crisis and phaeochromocytoma surgery
subtitle: Hydrocortisone now; alpha-block before the knife

sources.title: Society for Endocrinology Endocrine Emergency Guidance: emergency management of acute adrenal insufficiency (adrenal crisis) in adult patients (Arlt W, Endocr Connect)

sources.org: Association of Anaesthetists, Royal College of Physicians and Society for Endocrinology
sources.title: Guidelines for the management of glucocorticoids during the peri-operative period for patients with adrenal insufficiency (Woodcock T et al., Anaesthesia)
Pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma: an Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline (Lenders JWM et al., J Clin Endocrinol Metab)

sources.org: European Society of Endocrinology (ESE) and European Network for the Study of Adrenal Tumors (ENSAT)
sources.title: Management of adrenal incidentalomas: European Society of Endocrinology clinical practice guideline (Fassnacht M et al., Eur J Endocrinol)

red_flags.text: Hypotension unresponsive to fluids or vasopressors in a patient on long-term steroids, or after adrenalectomy: adrenal crisis.
Vomiting, abdominal pain, confusion, hyponatraemia or hyperkalaemia in a patient with known adrenal insufficiency.
Paroxysmal headache, sweating, palpitations and hypertension, or hypertension provoked by induction or abdominal palpation: undiagnosed phaeochromocytoma.
Any adrenal mass about to be biopsied or removed without biochemical exclusion of phaeochromocytoma.
Hypotension and hypoglycaemia in the hours after phaeochromocytoma removal.

do_now.text: Suspected adrenal crisis: hydrocortisone 100 mg IV or IM immediately, followed by 200 mg over 24 hours by continuous infusion (or 50 mg IV or IM every six hours).
Rapid rehydration with 1 litre of 0.9% saline over the first hour, then guided by the patient's response, with cardiac monitoring.
Do not delay hydrocortisone for tests. Take blood for cortisol and ACTH if it can be done without delay.

Surgery in a patient with adrenal insufficiency or on long-term glucocorticoids: hydrocortisone 100 mg IV at induction, then 200 mg over 24 hours by infusion or 50 mg every six hours, while nil by mouth.
Never biopsy or operate on an adrenal mass until phaeochromocytoma has been excluded with plasma free or urinary fractionated metanephrines.

assess.text: Steroid history: dose, duration and route, including inhaled, topical and intra-articular steroids, which can all suppress the axis.
Sodium, potassium, glucose and renal function; hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia support adrenal insufficiency.
Phaeochromocytoma preparation: seated and standing blood pressure and heart rate, symptoms, and evidence of catecholamine cardiomyopathy.

investigate.text: Plasma free metanephrines or urinary fractionated metanephrines for any suspected phaeochromocytoma or any adrenal incidentaloma.
Cross-sectional imaging after biochemical confirmation, not before; functional imaging when metastatic or multifocal disease is suspected.
Genetic testing should be considered for all patients with phaeochromocytoma or paraganglioma.
Echocardiography in long-standing or severe catecholamine excess.

resuscitate.text: Phaeochromocytoma: alpha-adrenergic blockade for 7 to 14 days before surgery, with a high-sodium diet and generous fluid intake to restore intravascular volume.
Add a beta-blocker for tachycardia only after adequate alpha-blockade. Beta-blockade first risks a hypertensive crisis from unopposed alpha stimulation.
Target before surgery: blood pressure below 130/80 mmHg seated, with systolic above 90 mmHg standing, and heart rate around 60 to 70 seated and 70 to 80 standing.

definitive.text: Adrenalectomy for phaeochromocytoma by an experienced endocrine surgeon and anaesthetist, usually laparoscopic, with invasive arterial monitoring and vasoactive drugs ready for surges during tumour handling.
After removal, monitor blood pressure, heart rate and blood glucose for 24 to 48 hours: hypotension and rebound hypoglycaemia are expected risks.
After unilateral adrenalectomy for cortisol excess, or bilateral adrenalectomy, give glucocorticoid replacement and plan a supervised wean or lifelong replacement.
After recovery from adrenal crisis, convert to oral double-dose replacement then taper, and educate on sick-day rules and an emergency injection kit.

escalate.text: Endocrinology and critical care for adrenal crisis that does not respond quickly.
Phaeochromocytoma surgery belongs in a unit with experienced endocrine surgeons and anaesthetists; transfer rather than operate occasionally.
Stop the operation and treat if an unexpected hypertensive crisis occurs during handling of an undiagnosed adrenal or retroperitoneal mass.

notes: In adrenal crisis the drug is cheap and safe and the delay is lethal. Give hydrocortisone on suspicion.
Alpha first, beta second. The order matters more than the choice of drug.
Every adrenal incidentaloma is a phaeochromocytoma until the metanephrines say otherwise. A needle in an untreated phaeochromocytoma can kill.
